A1.1.2: What gives a water molecule partial charges?
Oxygen attracts the shared electrons more strongly than hydrogen. Oxygen is partially negative and each hydrogen is partially positive.
A1.1.3: What is the difference between cohesion and adhesion in water?
Cohesion is attraction between water molecules. Adhesion is attraction between water and a different surface.
A1.2.2: What are the three components of a nucleotide?
A phosphate group, a five-carbon sugar and a nitrogenous base.
A1.2.4: Which base is used in RNA in place of thymine?
A2.1.2: Why do viruses depend on cells for reproduction?
Viruses lack the cellular machinery needed to make their own proteins and use a host cell to make new virus particles.
A2.1.4: What did the Miller–Urey experiment show?
Some organic molecules, including amino acids, can form without living organisms under the conditions simulated. The experiment did not produce life.
A2.2.2: How do you calculate magnification from an image?
Divide image size by actual size, using the same units for both.
A2.2.4: Which four structures or materials do all cells have in common?
A plasma membrane, cytoplasm, DNA and ribosomes.
A2.3.1: The protein coat that encloses a virus's genetic material.
A2.3.2: A lipid membrane surrounding the capsid in some viruses.
A3.1.3: How do you write a binomial species name?
Write the genus with a capital letter, then the specific epithet in lowercase. Italicize both words in typed text.
A3.1.4: Why is the biological species concept difficult to apply to fossils?
You cannot directly test whether fossil organisms could interbreed and produce fertile offspring.
A3.2.3: What makes two biological features homologous?
They have a shared evolutionary origin, even if they now perform different functions.
A3.2.4: Which organisms must a monophyletic group include?
A common ancestor and all of its descendants.
A4.1.1: What changes in a population when it evolves?
The frequency of inherited variants changes across generations.
A4.1.5: Independent evolution of similar features in different lineages, often under similar selection pressures.
A4.2.4: How can habitat fragmentation reduce gene flow?
It can isolate populations in separate patches, making movement and breeding between them less likely.
A4.2.5: Two sites each have four species. Can they differ in evenness?
Yes. The site with more similar abundances across its four species has greater evenness.
B1.1.2: Which reaction joins two monosaccharides, and what does it release?
Condensation forms a glycosidic bond and releases water.
B1.1.3: What is water's role in hydrolysis?
Water is used to break a bond, splitting a larger molecule into smaller products.
B1.2.2: Which groups react to form a peptide bond?
The carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of another.
B1.2.5: Why can denaturation stop an enzyme from working?
Denaturation changes the protein's shape, which can change the active site and impair substrate binding or catalysis.
B2.1.3: In which direction does a substance move by simple diffusion?
Its net movement is from higher to lower concentration. Simple diffusion uses no ATP.
B2.1.5: In which direction does water move by osmosis?
Across a selectively permeable membrane, net water movement is from higher to lower water potential.
B2.2.2: How does RNA leave the nucleus?
It passes through nuclear pores in the nuclear envelope.
B2.2.3: How does compartmentalization help enzymes work?
Membranes can maintain different conditions, such as pH, in separate compartments so different enzymes can work efficiently.
B2.3.2: Which two abilities define a stem cell?
It can self-renew through division and differentiate into specialized cell types.
B2.3.4: How does pluripotency differ from multipotency?
Pluripotent cells can form cell types from all three embryonic germ layers. Multipotent cells can form several, usually related, cell types.
B3.1.1: What happens to the surface-area-to-volume ratio as a body grows without changing shape?
It decreases because volume increases faster than surface area.
B3.1.3: What is the difference between ventilation and perfusion?
Ventilation moves air or water past an exchange surface. Perfusion supplies blood to that surface. Both help maintain diffusion gradients.
B3.2.2: What determines whether a blood vessel is an artery or a vein?
Direction of blood flow. Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins carry blood toward it.
B3.2.5: How do skeletal muscles and valves help return venous blood to the heart?
Muscle contractions squeeze nearby veins, and one-way valves prevent backflow.
B3.3.2: During a sarcomere contraction, do actin and myosin filaments shorten?
No. They slide past each other, increasing overlap and bringing the Z lines closer together.
B3.3.4: What makes up one motor unit?
One motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it innervates.
B4.1.2: How can aerial roots help a mangrove in waterlogged sediment?
They allow oxygen to reach root tissues where the surrounding sediment contains little oxygen.
B4.1.4: When is a transect useful in a habitat survey?
When you want to measure how species occurrence or abundance changes along an environmental gradient.
B4.2.1: What does an ecological niche describe beyond an organism's location?
How it uses resources, interacts with other organisms and tolerates environmental conditions.
B4.2.5: An organism that can combine autotrophic and heterotrophic ways of obtaining nutrition.
C1.1.1: What does an enzyme change about a reaction's energy profile?
It lowers the activation energy without changing the overall free-energy change or equilibrium position.
C1.1.5: Binding changes the shape of the enzyme's active site, helping it catalyse the reaction.
C1.2.2: What are the usual products of ATP hydrolysis in cells?
ADP and inorganic phosphate. Coupling ATP hydrolysis to other reactions can drive energy-requiring processes.
C1.2.4: Where in a eukaryotic cell do glycolysis and the Krebs cycle occur?
Glycolysis occurs in the cytosol; the Krebs cycle occurs in the mitochondrial matrix.
C1.3.3: Does oxygen released in photosynthesis come from carbon dioxide or water?
Water. Its splitting in the light-dependent reactions releases oxygen.
C1.3.4: How do you calculate an Rf value in chromatography?
Divide the distance travelled by the pigment by the distance travelled by the solvent front, measuring both from the origin.
C2.1.3: What does a second messenger do?
It relays a signal inside the cell after a receptor is activated. Cyclic AMP is one example.
C2.1.5: Why does the same circulating hormone affect only certain cells?
Only cells with a suitable receptor can directly respond to that hormone.
C2.2.2: How does the sodium–potassium pump maintain ion gradients?
It uses ATP to move three Na⁺ ions out of the cell and two K⁺ ions in per cycle.
C2.2.4: The action potential is regenerated at successive nodes of Ranvier, speeding conduction along a myelinated axon.
C3.1.2: A property that arises from the interaction of parts and is absent in the parts on their own.
C3.1.5: What is the basic signal path in a withdrawal reflex?
A receptor detects the stimulus, a sensory neuron carries the signal into the spinal cord, and a motor neuron activates an effector muscle.
C3.2.2: How do mucus and cilia work together in the airways?
Mucus traps particles and microorganisms. Cilia move the mucus toward the throat.
C3.2.4: Why is a secondary adaptive immune response often faster?
Memory cells from the first exposure can respond more rapidly when they recognize the same antigen again.
C4.1.3: When are quadrats useful for estimating abundance?
For sessile or slow-moving organisms. Randomly placed quadrats give samples that can be scaled to a larger area.
C4.1.5: The population size that an environment can sustain over time under its available resources and conditions.
C4.2.2: What provides energy for chemosynthetic producers?
Energy released by oxidizing inorganic substances, such as hydrogen sulfide.
C4.2.4: Which way does an arrow point in a food web?
From the organism eaten to the consumer, showing the direction of energy transfer.
D1.1.2: What does semi-conservative DNA replication conserve in each daughter molecule?
One strand from the original DNA molecule. The other strand is newly synthesized.
D1.1.3: What separates complementary DNA strands during replication?
Helicase separates the strands by disrupting hydrogen bonds between complementary bases.
D1.2.1: Which enzyme makes RNA during transcription?
RNA polymerase joins RNA nucleotides using one DNA strand as a template.
D1.2.5: What is the immediate product of translation?
A polypeptide. It may need to fold or be modified before it becomes functional.
D1.3.2: Why can a base substitution be synonymous?
More than one codon can encode the same amino acid, so the changed codon can specify the same amino acid.
D1.3.3: Which insertions or deletions shift a reading frame?
Those in a coding sequence that add or remove a number of nucleotides that is not a multiple of three.
D2.1.2: How does cytokinesis differ in plant and animal cells?
Plant cells form a cell plate that develops into a new partition. Animal cells pinch inward at a cleavage furrow.
D2.1.5: A cell has 2n = 4. How many chromosomes and chromatids does it have just after S phase?
Four chromosomes and eight chromatids. Each replicated chromosome still counts as one until its sister chromatids separate.
D2.2.3: What happens to mRNA abundance if degradation increases and transcription stays constant?
The steady-state mRNA abundance generally falls because transcripts are removed faster.
D2.2.4: How does epigenetic regulation differ from mutation?
Epigenetic regulation can change gene activity without changing the DNA base sequence. A mutation changes the sequence.
D2.3.2: What happens to a cell's water content in a hypotonic solution?
Water enters the cell by osmosis, so its water content increases.
D2.3.3: Does water stop crossing a cell membrane in an isotonic solution?
No. Water continues moving both ways, but there is no net movement.
D3.1.2: What happens to chromosome number at fertilization?
Two haploid gametes fuse to form a diploid zygote.
D3.2.3: What makes a genotype heterozygous at one locus?
The organism has two different alleles at that locus.
D3.2.5: What genotype ratio is expected from Aa × Aa?
1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, assuming normal segregation and equal survival.
D3.3.2: The response opposes the initial change and brings the regulated variable back toward its usual range.
D3.3.3: Which hormone lowers blood glucose, and which raises it?
Insulin lowers blood glucose. Glucagon raises it, mainly by acting on the liver.
D4.1.2: Which process creates new alleles, and which reshuffles existing alleles?
Mutation creates new alleles. Recombination reshuffles existing alleles.
D4.1.5: By relative reproductive success: how much an individual contributes to subsequent generations compared with others.
D4.2.1: How do resistance and resilience differ in ecology?
Resistance is how little a system changes during a disturbance. Resilience is its capacity to recover afterward.
D4.2.5: What makes a species a keystone species?
It has an effect on the ecosystem that is disproportionately large relative to its abundance.
D4.3.1: How do greenhouse gases affect Earth's outgoing radiation?
They absorb and re-emit some outgoing infrared radiation, reducing the rate of heat loss to space at first.
D4.3.2: Why does melting sea ice amplify warming?
Open water reflects less sunlight than ice. It absorbs more energy, increasing warming and encouraging more ice melt.
